strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.20.8	Evening wage for vineyard workers	The commentary's afternoon laborer reaches payday as the day ends; the vineyard owner calls the workers at evening to receive wages, making the daily deadline concrete.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.20.12	One hour versus full day's labor	The late workers have worked only one hour, while others bore the whole day's burden; the contrast sharpens the commentary's question of time spent and recompense.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.20.9	Pay for eleventh-hour workers	The workers hired at the eleventh hour receive a denarius; payment after little remaining daylight complicates any simple equation of duration and wage.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.9.4	Work while it is day	Jesus says work must be done during daylight because night comes when no one can work; this gives the commentary's closing workday a direct moral deadline.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.24.15	Wages before sunset	The hired poor worker's wage must be paid that day before the sun sets, providing a legal counterpart to the commentary's afternoon and due wage.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Hag.1.6	Wages in a bag with holes	Workers earn wages only to put them in a pierced purse; the commentary's capital eaten away by passing time becomes an image of labor without retained gain.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Mark.8.36	Gain world lose soul	Jesus asks what it profits a person to gain the whole world and forfeit life; the commentary's losing capital ultimately means losing the self.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.12.20	Rich fool's soul required tonight	The rich man's accumulated goods cannot extend the deadline when his life is required that night; this closely meets the commentary's hoarder who thinks property lengthens life.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.12.21	Stored wealth and poverty toward God	The parable concludes that storing for oneself leaves one poor toward God; it supplies the distinction between a full earthly account and lasting gain.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.11.4	Wealth cannot profit on judgment day	The proverb says riches do not profit in the day of wrath but righteousness rescues from death; it gives the commentary's failed trade a final accounting.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.6.27	Labor for food that endures	Jesus contrasts labor for perishing food with food enduring to eternal life; the commentary likewise asks which expenditure of finite work survives.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Gal.6.9	Good work and harvest in due season	The community must not tire of doing good, because it will reap in due time if it does not give up; good action, patience, and deferred pay meet in one verse.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.3.8	Wage according to labor	Paul says planter and waterer each receive wages according to their labor; this directly joins the commentary's intentional work and earned payment.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.3.15	Work lost at reckoning	Paul says a builder whose work burns suffers loss though the person is saved; it distinguishes lost work from lost self in the commentary's final account.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2John.1.8	Lose work or receive full reward	The readers are warned to watch themselves so their labor is not lost and they receive a full reward; it binds vigilance, loss, and complete payment.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.14.13	Rest from labors, deeds follow	The dead in the Lord rest from labor and their deeds follow them; the wage scene acquires a precise boundary between ended labor and surviving deeds.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.22.12	Coming with recompense for work	The coming speaker brings payment to repay each according to work; it matches the commentary's final rather than immediate settlement.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.1.3	Profit from toil under the sun	Ecclesiastes asks what gain people have from all the toil they perform under the sun; the same accounting question frames life as spent effort.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.2.11	Works inspected, no gain	The speaker surveys all the work his hands made and finds no lasting profit under the sun; it is a concrete contrary ledger to profitable moral work.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.90.10	Years consumed by toil	Psalm 90 measures the human span and says its strength is toil and trouble that soon flies away; finite time and labor are the commentary's spent capital.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.90.12	Counting days toward wisdom	The prayer asks to be taught to number days so as to gain a wise heart; counting the finite resource of time answers the commentary's running loss.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.7.2	Hired worker waiting for wage	Job compares himself to a hired worker longing for his wages; the commentary's wage at the end of the workday has a biblical sufferer's voice.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.14.6	Hired laborer's day	Job asks God to look away until the mortal finishes the day like a hired worker; the comparison joins life's fixed span to an end-of-day wage.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.11.1	False balance and honest weight	A deceptive scale is abominable and a just weight pleasing to God; the commentary's short-weighted customer becomes an explicit moral violation.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Amos.8.5	Shrink measure, enlarge price, falsify scales	Merchants impatient for sacred time to end make the grain measure small and the price large; market hours and short measure meet exactly as in the commentary.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Lev.19.35	Injustice in measurements	The law forbids wronging another in measuring length, weight, or quantity; the commentary's deficit on the scale is a named social wrong.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Lev.19.36	Honest scales and weights	The command supplies just scales, just weights, and honest measures; these specify what the commentary's mutual right requires at a sale.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.25.15	Full measure prolongs days	The demand for a complete and just weight is attached to prolonged days in the land; measured fairness and the duration of life intersect.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mic.6.11	Can wicked scales be acquitted	The prophet asks whether dishonest scales and a bag of false weights can be counted clean; short weighing becomes a judicial question of right.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.6.38	Full measure poured back	The giver receives a good, pressed, overflowing measure, and the measure used is returned; it reworks the commentary's short measure into ample recompense.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.19.17	Lending to God by aiding the poor	The person who is gracious to the poor lends to the Lord, who repays the deed; God as counterparty and the other person's due converge.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.9	Use passing wealth for enduring welcome	Jesus says to make friends by means of unrighteous wealth so they receive one into eternal dwellings when it fails; finite capital can be spent for an enduring return.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.6.20	Treasure that does not decay	Treasure kept in heaven is beyond moth, rust, and thieves; it answers the commentary's contrast between exhausted human holdings and what endures with God.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Tim.6.19	Stored foundation for coming age	The wealthy are urged to store a good foundation for the future and take hold of real life; the commentary's altered investment of wealth has a close analogue.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.10.2	Wrongful treasure fails, righteousness rescues	Treasures gained wickedly profit nothing while righteousness delivers from death; moral action is the profitable alternative to a full but failing purse.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Phil.3.7	Former gains counted loss	Paul counts what had been gains as loss for Christ; it gives the commentary's profit-and-loss vocabulary a deliberate reversal of value.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Phil.3.8	Lose everything to gain Christ	Paul accepts the loss of all things to gain Christ; the text distinguishes chosen material loss from the commentary's ruinous loss of self.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.13.46	Merchant buys one costly pearl	The merchant sells all he has to buy the uniquely valuable pearl; surrendering capital becomes a successful transaction, beside the commentary's saving trade.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.3.18	Buy refined gold from the speaker	The speaker counsels a materially self-satisfied church to buy gold from him so it becomes rich; true capital is defined against apparent wealth.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.3.13	Day exposes quality of work	Paul says the Day reveals each builder's work and tests what sort it is; the commentary's payday includes judgment of the work itself.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.3.14	Enduring work receives reward	Work that survives the test brings its worker a reward; it supplies the positive balance opposite the loss in the adjoining verse.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Gal.6.8	Two investments, two harvests	Sowing to flesh yields decay while sowing to Spirit yields eternal life; the commentary's competing trades have concrete divergent returns.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.6.10	Work remembered by a just payer	God is not unjust to forget work and love shown in service to the saints; the wage due for good work is backed by divine justice.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.6.12	Faith and patience inherit promise	The audience is told to imitate those who inherit promises through faith and patience; two terms of the surah's exception become conditions of deferred receipt.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.2.7	Persistence in good work seeks immortality	People who persist in good action seek glory and immortality and receive eternal life; patient work answers the hoarder's false bid for immortality.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.15.58	Labor not in vain	Paul urges steadfastness and abundance in the Lord's work, knowing that labor is not empty; the commentary's loss versus enduring wage is stated directly.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Thess.1.3	Work of faith and endurance of hope	Paul remembers the congregation's work produced by faith and endurance sustained by hope; faith, deed, and patient continuation are inseparable.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.2.19	Faith, service, endurance, growing works	The speaker knows this church's works, faith, service, and endurance, and says its later works exceed earlier ones; the surah's exception is matched in a timed communal assessment.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.2.17	Faith without deeds is dead	James says faith by itself is dead if it lacks works; it makes the commentary's paired believing and intentional good action a necessary conjunction.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1John.3.18	Love in deed and truth	The community is told to love in action and truth, rather than merely in words; it specifies how mutual commitment to truth becomes practiced good.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.3.13	Exhort one another each day	The addressees must exhort one another daily while it is called today, lest anyone harden through deceit; mutual counsel has the commentary's passing-time urgency.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.10.24	Provoke one another to good deeds	The congregation must consider how to stir one another to love and good works; it is a direct communal form of the commentary's reciprocal exhortation.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Thess.5.14	Patiently admonish and help one another	The congregation is urged to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with all; the counsel to patience takes concrete social form.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Eph.4.25	Truth owed to fellow members	Each should speak truth with a neighbor because they belong to one another; the commentary's truth as an obligation owed across the community has a textual counterpart.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Eph.4.28	Work honestly to share with the needy	The former thief must work with his hands at what is good so he has something to share with one in need; intentional labor becomes another person's due.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.5.4	Withheld laborers' wages cry out	The wages kept from harvest workers cry out to the Lord of hosts; it specifies the wrong of failing to pay when work is done.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.5.7	Farmer waits patiently for harvest	The addressees are told to be patient until the Lord's coming as a farmer waits for precious fruit; deferred yield and endurance meet in a work scene.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.5.8	Strengthen hearts, coming near	The audience must also be patient and firm because the Lord's coming is near; it makes the promised settlement, rather than waiting alone, the point.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.22.13	Neighbor's labor without wages	The prophet condemns building a house by injustice while making a neighbor work for nothing and not giving wages; labor, rights, and payment join explicitly.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Lev.19.13	Hired worker's pay not held overnight	The law forbids retaining a hired worker's wages until morning; it sets an enforceable due time for the commentary's worker.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.10.7	Worker deserves pay	Jesus instructs envoys to accept a host's provision because the worker deserves wages; the commentary's wage is treated as a right, not a gift.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Tim.5.18	Laborer worthy of wage	The letter cites the maxim that the laborer deserves wages in a discussion of support for elders; earned pay is an obligation of the beneficiary.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.21.5	Patient planning yields profit	The plans of the diligent lead to profit, while haste leads to poverty; this specifies how intention and duration change the trade's result.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.13.11	Wealth accumulated gradually	Wealth gained rapidly shrinks, but gathering little by little increases it; the passage counters the commentary's image of a balance steadily diminishing.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.23.4	Do not exhaust oneself for riches	The proverb warns against toiling to acquire wealth; it challenges the worker who gives finite strength to a capital that cannot secure life.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.23.5	Wealth flies away	When one looks at riches they are gone, flying away like an eagle; it gives the commentary's vanishing earthly capital a sudden image.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.5.14	Wealth lost in a bad venture	Ecclesiastes describes riches lost through a bad business affair, leaving nothing for a child; the loss of principal and family consequence are both present.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.5.15	No earnings carried out of life	A person leaves this life as naked as at birth and carries nothing gained by toil; the commentary's trader cannot take the day's proceeds past death.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.9.10	Do the work before death	One must do with strength whatever the hand finds because no work or planning is done in Sheol; it makes a finite work period ethically urgent.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.12.14	Every work called to judgment	God will bring every deed, even hidden ones, to judgment; the commentary's final pay is based on a complete account of work.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.127.2	Early and late anxious toil	The psalm depicts rising early and sitting late to eat bread of painful toil while God gives sleep; it tests whether long hours alone secure gain.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mal.3.14	What profit in serving God	The speakers say service to God is vain and ask what gain comes from keeping his charge; the market question is raised within moral work itself.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mal.3.16	People speak together, remembered by God	Those who fear the Lord speak with one another and a book of remembrance is written for them; mutual counsel is entered into a lasting account.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mal.3.18	Serving God shown apart from not serving	God promises a visible distinction between the righteous and wicked, one serving him and one not; it answers the preceding dispute over the profit of service.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.37.3	Trust and do good together	The psalm joins trust in the Lord with doing good and dwelling securely; belief and beneficial action occupy one instruction.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.15.6	Belief counted as righteousness	Abram believes the Lord, who counts it to him as righteousness; faith is entered as a positive item in a divine account.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.15.1	God as great reward	The divine word tells Abram not to fear and promises great reward; a promised recompense precedes Abram's believing response later in the scene.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.11.6	Belief in God as rewarder	The passage requires one approaching God to believe he exists and rewards seekers; trust and eventual payment are deliberately linked.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.3.10	Eat the fruit of deeds	The righteous are told that things will go well because they will eat the fruit of their own actions; it puts moral labor and due return together.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.3.11	Evil deed returned upon doer	The wicked are told they will receive what their hands have done; this is the negative entry in the commentary's wage account.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.25.19	Master settles investment accounts	After a long time, the master returns to reckon with servants entrusted with talents; passing time and entrusted capital end in an account.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.25.16	Servant trades entrusted talents	The first servant trades the master's five talents and makes five more; the commentary's believer as faithful trader has a concrete scene.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.25.21	Faithful steward rewarded	The master calls the profitable servant good and faithful and sets him over more; profitable dealing is judged as trustworthiness.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.19.13	Trade until the owner's return	A nobleman gives money to servants and orders them to do business until he comes back; the commentary's market stays open for a limited absence.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.19.15	Owner asks each trade's gain	At his return the owner summons the servants to learn what they gained by trading; it is a direct closing of the ledger after elapsed time.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.11	Trustworthy with unrighteous wealth	Jesus asks who will entrust true riches to those unfaithful with worldly wealth; handling temporary capital becomes a test of entrusted responsibility.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.4.2	Stewards must be trustworthy	The requirement for a steward is to be found faithful; it supplies a concrete office for the commentary's trust opposed to betrayal.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Tim.6.17	Uncertain riches versus living God	The rich are told not to hope in uncertain riches but in God; it corrects the illusion that one's holdings can secure a future.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Tim.6.18	Good works as rich generosity	The wealthy are directed to be rich in good works and ready to share; it defines the alternate capital that the next verse stores for the future.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.4.16	Outer loss, inner renewal	The outer person wastes away while the inner is renewed daily; the commentary's continual expenditure of mortal capital need not entail loss of the person.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.4.18	Temporary seen, lasting unseen	The visible things are temporary and the unseen eternal; this supplies a specific axis for finite holdings versus enduring return.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.11.6	Sow morning and evening	In the morning one sows, and at evening one must not let the hand rest, since one cannot know which work succeeds; action continues up to the day's boundary.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.27.24	Riches do not last forever	The proverb asks whether riches or a crown persist through generations; it rebukes confidence that stored money outlasts mortal time.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Acts.3.1	Ninth-hour prayer	Peter and John go to the temple at the ninth hour, explicitly an hour of prayer; this is a concrete afternoon prayer beside the commentary's asr prayer.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Acts.10.30	Ninth-hour prayer at home	Cornelius recalls praying in his house at the ninth hour; it shows the afternoon prayer time in another early Christian setting.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Acts.10.4	Prayer and alms remembered	Cornelius is told his prayers and alms have come before God as a memorial; the afternoon prayer scene's charity is kept in a divine account.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Berakhot 4:1	Afternoon prayer's deadline	The mishnah assigns a latest time to the afternoon prayer, with a reported disagreement over its extent; it contextualizes the commentary's named afternoon prayer as timed practice.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 2:15	Day short, work great, wage great	Rabbi Tarfon's saying calls the day short, work great, workers sluggish, and reward abundant; the commentary's entire daily labor image is compressed here.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 2:16	Trustworthy employer pays worker	The continuation says the employer is trustworthy to pay for labor and places the righteous person's reward in the future; it joins amanah, wage, and delayed payment.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 3:16	Open shop and written ledger	The parable's shop extends credit while a written ledger and collectors bring every debt to account; it mirrors the commentary's open market and mutual obligations.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 4:16	Prepare in vestibule before entering	The present life is a vestibule where one prepares for the coming hall; finite preparatory time precedes the lasting result of work.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 4:17	One hour of deeds before the next world	The saying values one hour of repentance and good deeds in this life above the whole coming life, giving a sharp reason to use remaining time now.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.1.3	Arabic ص ل ح / Hebrew צלח, table sound correspondence only	The tree bears fruit in its season and prospers in all it does; the table's Hebrew root means prospering, a suggestive but unverified sound link to the commentary's salih deeds and timed reward.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Josh.1.8	Arabic ص ل ح / Hebrew צלח, table sound correspondence only	Keeping and meditating on the law day and night makes one's way prosper; the sound-corresponding Hebrew verb links success to sustained obedient conduct, though Arabic salih here means good deeds.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Gen.39.3	Arabic ص ل ح / Hebrew צלח, table sound correspondence only	Potiphar sees the Lord prosper all that Joseph does; the Hebrew success verb gives the commentary's evaluated work a narrative example without proving cognacy.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Gen.39.23	Arabic ص ل ح / Hebrew צלח, table sound correspondence only	Joseph's prison keeper need not inspect what is entrusted to him, and the Lord prospers his work; trust, labor, and successful outcome converge with the source's secondary marketplace scene.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Dan.6.29	Arabic ص ل ح / Aramaic צלח, table sound correspondence only	Daniel prospers under Darius and Cyrus after surviving a trial of fidelity; the Aramaic prosperity verb is a cautious sound link to the commentary's salih outcome.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Exod.17.12	Arabic ء م ن / Hebrew אמנ, table sound correspondence only	Moses' hands remain steady until sunset because Aaron and Hur support them; the Hebrew faithfulness root physically joins supported endurance to an evening boundary.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Hab.2.4	Arabic ء م ن / Hebrew אמנ, table sound correspondence only	The righteous lives by faithfulness while the proud one is not upright; the table's Hebrew firmness root adds fidelity over time to the commentary's believing exception.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.111.7	Arabic ء م ن / Hebrew אמנ, table sound correspondence only	Works of God's hands are truth and justice and his precepts are trustworthy; the Hebrew root ties reliability to deeds and right order rather than assent alone.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.111.8	Arabic ء م ن / Hebrew אמנ, table sound correspondence only	The precepts are established forever and done in truth and uprightness; the table's firmness family gives a lasting counterpart to transient human accounts.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Prov.12.22	Arabic ء م ن / Hebrew אמנ, table sound correspondence only	God delights in people who act faithfully while lying lips offend; the shared consonants connect the commentary's trust opposed to betrayal with actual conduct.
